title: Parallel Execution ThreadLocal Memory Leak
options: quitDriver() calls quit() but never calls driverTL.remove(). After quit(), the ThreadLocal still references an invalid WebDriver. The next test on the same thread sees a non-null driver (because remove() was never called), returns the stale session, and fails. When BeforeMethod throws an exception, AfterMethod is skipped entirely, so driverTL.remove() never runs. The leaked driver reference accumulates in the Thread's ThreadLocalMap, preventing GC. After ~200 iterations, retained heap from undead Chrome process references causes OutOfMemoryError and new thread creation fails.

The --headless=new flag in Chrome 112+ has a known memory fragmentation bug when browser instances are created and destroyed rapidly in sequence on the same JVM. After ~200 sequential create/quit cycles, Chrome's zygote process leaks anonymous page table entries that the OS cannot reclaim, causing mmap to fail and new sessions to crash with 'Unable to create new native thread'.

TestNG reuses threads from a fixed pool. After ~25 tests per thread (~200 total), the JVM's CodeCache fills with dynamically generated bytecode from ChromeDriver's W3C protocol deserialization layer. The JVM enters a continuous safepoint-ops loop trying to free CodeCache, which pauses all application threads for 500ms-2s. These pauses cause Chrome's CDP socket connections to time out, resulting in cascading session failures.

ChromeDriver constructor negotiates the protocol version via a bidirectional JSON-over-HTTP exchange on a randomly assigned TCP port. With 8 concurrent thread creations, the OS TCP ephemeral port range (32768-60999 on Linux) is exhausted after ~200 iterations per agent, causing bind() to fail with EADDRINUSE and preventing new ChromeDriver sessions from being created.

title: Implicit + Explicit Wait Anti-Pattern in Selenium 4
options: Selenium 4 enforces W3C WebDriver protocol compliance. Under W3C, the implicit wait timeout is sent as a session parameter and is applied by the browser driver's HTTP handler on every findElement operation -- including those triggered internally by ExpectedConditions. Each poll of elementToBeClickable calls findElement internally, which now blocks for up to 10s. With default 500ms polling, a single poll cycle takes 10.5s, so the 15s explicit wait completes only 1-2 poll attempts instead of 30. Between those sparse detections and the final findElement+click(), React's virtual DOM diffing invalidates the element reference.

Selenium 4's new relative locator API internally modifies the element cache behavior. When any test class imports or uses relative locators anywhere in the classpath, Selenium enables aggressive element cache pruning that evicts element references after 500ms. Combined with the implicit wait of 10s, the cache eviction race causes StaleElementReferenceException on every click interaction.

The combination worked in Selenium 3 because JWP (JSON Wire Protocol) returned raw element IDs that Selenium cached locally. Selenium 4's W3C protocol returns element references as maps with an 'element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf' key. Each findElement deserializes this map using Java reflection, which is 7x slower than Selenium 3's integer ID lookup. The cumulative deserialization time across 30 poll cycles causes the 3x slowdown.

Chrome 120+ changed the default behavior of elementToBeClickable to use 'scrollIntoViewIfNeeded' instead of 'scrollIntoView'. Combined with React's concurrent mode rendering, the scroll action triggers a re-render that replaces the element node in the DOM tree. The implicit wait delay of 10s makes this window wider, causing StaleElementReferenceException on every click.

title: Kafka Consumer Group Rebalance in Test Framework
options: With 50 consumers in the same group subscribed to a single topic, Kafka triggers a rebalance each time any consumer calls poll() -- because the consumer session heartbeat is blocked by the synchronous poll() call. With 50 threads all polling every 1s, the group coordinator sees continuous partition revocation and reassignment. Consumers spend more time rebalancing than consuming, and auto.offset.reset=latest means they may miss events produced during rebalance windows.

Setting enable.auto.commit=false without implementing manual commit in a finally block means that if an exception occurs in waitForEvent before commitSync() is called, the consumer will re-process the same records on the next poll. This causes duplicate event detection across threads, and each thread keeps seeing the same events, preventing forward progress.

The poll timeout of 1000ms is too short for a consumer group with 50 members. Kafka's max.poll.interval.ms defaults to 300s. Each consumer must call poll() within this interval or be considered dead. With 50 consumers, the rebalance time is O(n log n) in the number of partitions. The consumers exceed the rebalance timeout before stabilization, causing infinite rebalance loops.

Each PaymentValidator instance creates its own KafkaConsumer on a separate thread without coordination. The consumer group protocol requires one consumer per thread, but 50 consumers with max.poll.records=100 on a topic with fewer than 50 partitions means most consumers get 0 partitions assigned. Consumers with 0 partitions still participate in rebalances but never receive data, while consumers with 1+ partitions spend time committing offsets, triggering rebalances on any delay.
answer: With 50 consumers in the same group subscribed to a single topic, Kafka triggers a rebalance each time any consumer calls poll() -- because the consumer session heartbeat is blocked by the synchronous poll() call. With 50 threads all polling every 1s, the group coordinator sees continuous partition revocation and reassignment. Consumers spend more time rebalancing than consuming, and auto.offset.reset=latest means they may miss events produced during rebalance windows.

title: OAuth2 Token Refresh Race Condition in API Tests
options: In v5.0, expiresInSecs() returns the raw JWT 'exp' claim value -- a Unix epoch timestamp (e.g., 1719750000). The check expiresInSecs() < 300 compares a billion-scale epoch value against 300, which is always false. The token is never proactively refreshed. After exactly 3600 seconds, the token expires. All 16 threads race through the DCL. The first thread gets a new token in ~200ms but meanwhile the other 15 threads had already passed the null check with the old token. After the lock releases, they each see the new token but expiresInSecs() returns the epoch timestamp again -- always > 300 -- so they don't refetch. However, the first thread's new token was fetched at second 3600 exactly when the old token expired. The auth server's clock skew tolerance causes the new token to also be rejected for 1-2 seconds. All 16 calls fail with 401 simultaneously.

In v5.0, expiresInSecs() always returns 3600 (never decrements). The REFRESH_BUFFER check expiresInSecs() < 300 is never true. The token is never proactively refreshed. After 30 minutes, the token expires on the auth server. All 16 threads simultaneously detect expiry, race to synchronized fetchToken(), but the winner gets a new token. The 15 blocked threads each sequentially re-enter the synchronized block after the lock releases, see the new token, but expiresInSecs() still returns 3600 (raw value). They each unnecessarily fetch a new token -- 16 times sequentially -- causing 16 back-to-back POSTs. The first 14 succeed, but the 15th and 16th hit rate limiting, fail, return null, and all 16 threads get null on the next iteration.

In v4.3, expiresInSecs() returned System.currentTimeMillis() - issuedAt + expiresIn. In v5.0, it returns the literal expires_in field from the JSON response. When the library changed this, the deserialization of the token response changed from 'int' to 'long'. In Java, comparing a long to the int constant 300 in REFRESH_BUFFER causes a silent overflow when expires_in is a Unix timestamp in seconds (e.g., 1719750000), making the comparison effectively expiresInSecs() - 300 < 0, which incorrectly triggers refresh on every getToken() call. The 16 threads race through the DCL, all pass the first check, all block on synchronized, fetch 16 tokens sequentially, and the auth server throttles after the 10th concurrent request.

In v5.0, the AccessToken class changed equals() and hashCode() to include the raw JWT string. The getToken() method uses '!=' to compare the currentToken reference after the synchronized block returns. If fetchToken() in v5.0 returns a different object instance for the same JWT (due to caching changes), the reference comparison 'currentToken == null || currentToken.expiresInSecs()' passes the null check for the first thread, but the volatile read of currentToken may see a partially constructed object under the new memory model, returning a token with all-zero fields.

title: Chrome Docker Container OOM in K8s Selenium Grid
prompt:
Your Selenium Grid 4 is deployed on Kubernetes with 5 node pods, each requesting 4GB memory and 2 CPU cores. Each pod runs 4 Chrome browser slots. The team added 500 new tests (now 3,500 total). Tests start failing around test #1,800 with:

```
org.openqa.selenium.SessionNotCreatedException: Chrome failed to start: exited abnormally
  Chrome: cgroup memory limit reached
  [31866:31866:ERROR:broker_posix.cc(44)] Broker: ReceiveMessage failed: Connection reset by peer (104)
```

The K8s pod describe shows:
```
Containers:
  Limits:
    memory: "4Gi"
    cpu: "2"
  Requests:
    memory: "3.5Gi"
    cpu: "1.5"
```

Which intervention would MOST effectively resolve the failures with minimal infrastructure cost?
options: Increase each pod's memory limit from 4Gi to 8Gi. This gives each Chrome instance up to 2GB of headroom. The root cause is that 4 Chrome instances sharing 4GB exceed the memory limit when any test navigates to a heavy SPA page that leaks DOM nodes. Setting memory limits to 8Gi on the existing 5 pods provides the necessary buffer without changing the Grid topology.

Reduce the per-pod slot count from 4 to 2. Lower the request to 2Gi and limit to 3Gi. The root cause is that each Chrome instance consumes 800MB-1.5GB private RSS. With 4 slots per 4Gi pod, the OS + Selenium server + Chrome + ChromeDriver processes exceed the cgroup memory limit. Reducing to 2 slots per pod guarantees each Chrome instance has ~1.5GB. Add 5 more pods to maintain 20 total slots.

Add '--disable-dev-shm-usage' and '--memory-limit=1024' to ChromeOptions. The root cause is that /dev/shm is 64MB in Docker by default. Chrome uses /dev/shm for shared memory between the browser and renderer processes. With 4 Chrome instances sharing 64MB, each gets 16MB -- insufficient for modern web pages. Disabling /dev/shm usage makes Chrome use anonymous mmap instead, which respects the cgroup memory limit.

Set the K8s pod memory request equal to the limit (4Gi) and remove the 0.5Gi buffer gap. The root cause is that K8s overcommits memory when request < limit. The node scheduler packs additional pods onto the same node, causing the actual available memory per pod to be less than 4Gi. With request == limit, K8s guarantees the full 4Gi, preventing OOM kills.
answer: Reduce the per-pod slot count from 4 to 2. Lower the request to 2Gi and limit to 3Gi. The root cause is that each Chrome instance consumes 800MB-1.5GB private RSS. With 4 slots per 4Gi pod, the OS + Selenium server + Chrome + ChromeDriver processes exceed the cgroup memory limit. Reducing to 2 slots per pod guarantees each Chrome instance has ~1.5GB. Add 5 more pods to maintain 20 total slots.

title: SQL N+1 Query in Test Data Validation
options: Add database connection pooling (HikariCP) with max 20 connections and set batch fetch size to 1000. The root cause is that each db.query() call opens a new connection. With 10,000 customers * 4 queries = 40,000 connections, the connection overhead dominates. Connection pooling reuses connections and batch fetching reduces round trips.

Replace all N+1 queries with a single SQL join query that fetches all customer data, orders, payments, subscriptions, and order items in one round trip. Use a Java Stream to group results in memory. The root cause is the N+1 query pattern: 1 query for IDs + 10,000 * (3 entity queries + N order-item queries per customer) = 50,000+ queries. A single denormalized query with LEFT JOINs reduces this to 1 round trip.

Rewrite the validation using Java parallel streams and CompletableFuture. Execute the per-customer validation queries asynchronously using a thread pool of 32 threads. The root cause is single-threaded sequential execution that does not utilize the database server's parallel query capability.

Add database indexes on orders.customer_id, payments.customer_id, subscriptions.customer_id, and order_items.order_id. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on each query and confirm index-only scans. The root cause is full table scans on unindexed foreign key columns.
answer: Replace all N+1 queries with a single SQL join query that fetches all customer data, orders, payments, subscriptions, and order items in one round trip. Use a Java Stream to group results in memory. The root cause is the N+1 query pattern: 1 query for IDs + 10,000 * (3 entity queries + N order-item queries per customer) = 50,000+ queries. A single denormalized query with LEFT JOINs reduces this to 1 round trip.

title: React Shadow DOM Test Synchronization Failure
options: The presenceOfElementLocated check for the host element passes when the <checkout-card> tag is parsed by the HTML parser, but the shadowRoot is null at that point because React's createRoot() and the component's constructor which attaches the shadow root via attachShadow() run asynchronously in a microtask. The wait does not verify that shadowRoot is non-null. In CI (slower), the race window is wider. The fix: wait for shadowRoot !== null before finding elements inside it.

The issue is that findElement(By.cssSelector("checkout-card")) uses the Light DOM, but after Selenium 4, driver.findElement interacts with the flattened tree (including shadow roots) by default. The <checkout-card> found by findElement is actually the first element inside the shadow root, not the host. The executeScript then tries to call shadowRoot on an element that is already inside the shadow DOM, which returns null.

Shadow DOM v1 does not allow querying elements by CSS selector across shadow boundaries. The executeScript('return arguments[0].shadowRoot', host) traverses into the shadow root, but Selenium's By.cssSelector uses the page's global stylesheet scope. Even inside the shadow root, the subsequent findElement call leaves the shadow root's scope and searches the global DOM.

React 18's concurrent mode uses startTransition for the checkout flow, which defers the Shadow DOM attachment. The <checkout-card> element is present in the Light DOM immediately (rendered by React), but the attachShadow() call in the component's useEffect() is deferred as a Transition. In Rapid mode (dev machines), React completes the Transition quickly. In CI (slow), the Transition is interrupted by the test's polling.
answer: The presenceOfElementLocated check for the host element passes when the <checkout-card> tag is parsed by the HTML parser, but the shadowRoot is null at that point because React's createRoot() and the component's constructor which attaches the shadow root via attachShadow() run asynchronously in a microtask. The wait does not verify that shadowRoot is non-null. In CI (slower), the race window is wider. The fix: wait for shadowRoot !== null before finding elements inside it.

title: Retry Logic with Side Effects Causes Data Corruption
options: The problem: when the POST to /users returns 503, the retry loop submits the same request again. If the first request actually succeeded on the server (the 503 was a proxy timeout after the user was created), the retry creates a duplicate user with the same email. The 503 might be a gateway timeout after the server committed the transaction but before sending the response. The fix: use RestAssured's built-in retry with a request replay filter that reuses the same HTTP connection and detects idempotent methods. For non-idempotent POST, generate a unique idempotency key per initial attempt and resend the same key on retry.

The problem: Thread.sleep(2000) in the retry loop blocks the test thread but does not release the HTTP connection. With 16 parallel threads creating users simultaneously, the HttpClient connection pool is exhausted after 8 concurrent requests. Subsequent requests queue, exceed the 503 gateway timeout, and all fail.

The problem: the catch(Exception) block catches ALL exceptions including InterruptedException from Thread.sleep, which clears the thread's interrupt flag. When the same thread is reused by TestNG for the next test, the cleared interrupt flag causes the next Thread.sleep call in any retry logic to immediately throw InterruptedException, collapsing all subsequent retries.

The problem: RestAssured's .body(request) serializes the Java object each time the request is sent. If the UserRequest object's toString() or serialization produces a different JSON body on retry (due to a timestamp field set at construction time), the server creates two different users.

If the first request actually succeeded on the server (the 503 was a proxy timeout after the user was created), the retry creates a duplicate user with the same email. The 503 might be a gateway timeout after the server committed the transaction but before sending the response. The fix: use RestAssured's built-in retry with a request replay filter that reuses the same HTTP connection and detects idempotent methods. For non-idempotent POST, generate a unique idempotency key per initial attempt and resend the same key on retry.

title: Kubernetes Pod Eviction During Parallel Test Run
prompt:
A microservices test suite deploys 15 ephemeral test environments to Kubernetes as isolated namespaces. Tests create pods, run assertions, and tear down. At test #2,100 of 5,000, tests start failing with:

```
pod "test-validator-84f7b" evicted
  Status: Failed
  Reason: NodeShutdown
  Message: Node was in a state of shutdown
```

Other tests in the same namespace also fail with ImagePullBackOff and CrashLoopBackOff. The K8s cluster has 6 worker nodes (c5.2xlarge, 8 vCPU, 16GB RAM each). What is the MOST LIKELY root cause?
options: The test validator pods accumulate monitoring data and logs in emptyDir volumes backed by node memory (tmpfs). After ~2,100 test iterations across 15 namespaces, the accumulated emptyDir data on each node exceeds the kubelet's eviction threshold (default: 10% of node capacity = 1.6GB). The kubelet evicts pods with the highest memory usage to reclaim resources.

The test framework schedules 15 namespace deployments simultaneously. Each namespace creates multiple pods that hit the cluster's DNS resolution limits. CoreDNS is configured with 2 replicas but receives ~5,000 DNS queries per second from pod-to-service lookups. CoreDNS hits the maxConcurrent limit (default 1000), drops queries, and pods fail with 'Temporary failure in name resolution'. Kubernetes then reports the node as unhealthy and drains pods.

The c5.2xlarge nodes run out of available ENI IP addresses in the VPC subnet. Each pod in the test namespace gets a unique IP. After ~2,100 pods per node, the subnet's /20 CIDR (4091 IPs) is exhausted. New pods fail with 'failed to assign IP address'.

The test framework does not wait for previous namespace teardown to complete before deploying the next test environment. Pods in 'Terminating' state hold onto IP addresses and ConfigMap resources. After 2,100 test iterations, the API server's etcd store has accumulated 150,000+ objects causing the API server to hit its --max-requests-inflight limit.

After ~2,100 test iterations across 15 namespaces, the accumulated emptyDir data on each node exceeds the kubelet's eviction threshold (default: 10% of node capacity = 1.6GB). The kubelet evicts pods with the highest memory usage to reclaim resources.

options: All ~90 remaining tests detect the 401 simultaneously. The retry logic in each test calls AuthManager.login() concurrently -- 90 requests to the token endpoint within 1 second. title: Thread-Safe Singleton DriverFactory
FluentWait with Broken Condition
answer:
Bug 1: The static method waitForElementVisible references the non-static instance field 'private WebDriver driver'. The static method cannot access a non-static field -- NullPointerException at runtime.

Bug 2: StaleElementReferenceException inside the lambda causes a retry with 2s poll interval. In CI (slower), the element is more likely to be in the 'stale' state when the lambda executes. The 2s gap between polls causes 30-second timeouts that locally never happen.

Bug 3: clickWhenReady calls waitForElementVisible which returns an element, then calls click(). Between the return and click(), the element can go stale -- especially in React SPAs. CI's slower execution guarantees this race manifests.

Bug 4: 2s poll interval is too coarse. For pages that render in 200ms, the test waits 2s before the first check, then another 2s if stale.

Fixed approach:
```java
public static void clickWhenReady(WebDriver driver, By locator) {
    new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(30))
        .pollingEvery(Duration.ofMillis(500))
        .until(ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(locator))
        .click();
}
```

title: Parallel Test Data Collision
Memory Leak in Screenshot Utility
answer:
Bug 1 -- PRIMARY MEMORY LEAK: allScreenshots is an unbounded static ArrayList. After 500 failures, it holds 500 File references. But the real leak: attachToReport() reads each screenshot into a byte[] and passes a ByteArrayInputStream to Allure. Allure internally retains ALL InputStream references until report generation at end of CI run. 500 screenshots at ~500KB each = 250MB retained in heap.

Bug 2: screenshotCounter++ is NOT thread-safe. Two threads can generate the same filename. Files.copy with REPLACE_EXISTING silently overwrites. Plus the same path is added to allScreenshots twice, so cleanupOldScreenshots calls delete() on the same path multiple times (first succeeds, second fails).

Bug 3: cleanupOldScreenshots calls remove(0) in a loop on ArrayList (O(n^2), 124,750 shifts for 500 items). If this runs while attachToReport() is reading, ConcurrentModificationException.

Bug 4: Files.readAllBytes() loads entire file into contiguous byte array. 500 contiguous 500KB allocations fragment the heap (large objects bypass TLAB).

Bug 5: OutputType.FILE creates a temp file that is never deleted.

Fix: Use Allure.addAttachment with a File path (deferred read), not a byte array. Use ThreadLocal counter with UUID. Use ConcurrentLinkedQueue for allScreenshots.

```java
public static void attachToReport(String fileName) {
    Allure.addAttachment("Screenshot", "image/png", 
        (ThrowingRunnable<InputStream>) () -> new FileInputStream(fileName));
}
```

title: Enterprise Multi-Application Automation Framework Architecture

- Cross-browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge), cross-platform
- 50 concurrent threads parallel execution

```
|   |-- app-a/pages/ components/ api/ models/ workflows/ tests/
|   |-- app-b/ ... (10 total, each as Maven module)
|-- test-commons/ (listeners, annotations: @Smoke @Flaky @Quarantine)
|-- docker/ (Dockerfile multi-stage, docker-compose, k8s manifests)
|-- config/ (app-{env}.yaml, vault-policy.hcl)
|-- pipeline-scripts/ (github-actions.yaml, Jenkinsfile, azure-pipelines.yaml)
`-- test-output/ (reports, logs, screenshots, videos)
```

2. DESIGN PATTERNS:
- Page Object Model: apps/*/pages/ (encapsulates elements + actions)
- Dependency Injection (Guice): framework-core/di/ (@Inject driver, config, services)
- Factory: BrowserFactory (creates Chrome/Firefox/Edge drivers)
- Strategy: RetryStrategy (per-test/per-suite/never retry)
- Observer: TestNG listeners publish events to Allure, Slack, ELK
- Circuit Breaker: ApiValidator (fail fast on unhealthy downstream)
- Facade: apps/*/workflows/ (complex multi-page operations)
- Builder: ApiValidator (fluent API chain)
- ThreadLocal + Singleton: DriverManager (per-thread driver isolation)
- Registry: CleanupRegistry (thread-safe entity tracking for ordered teardown)
- Template Method: SQLSeeder (abstract seed/cleanup per app)

3. PARALLEL EXECUTION:
- Threading: TestNG thread pool (50 threads). Each thread owns ThreadLocal<WebDriver>.
- Isolation: Each thread has its own WebDriver, HTTP client, DB connection (HikariCP pool of 20).
- State Sharing: ConcurrentHashMap-based SharedContext for cross-thread state (e.g., order ID created in Test A, used in Test B).
- K8s: Each pod runs 4 browser slots. Pod anti-affinity spreads across nodes. HPA based on queue depth. Resource limits: 4GB RAM, 2 CPU per pod.
- CI Matrix: GitHub Actions matrix [app][browser], each cell runs Docker + Xvfb. Jenkins parallel stages per app.

4. SCALING 1->10 APPS:
- Each app is a Maven module inheriting parent POM. Adding app = 3 files: page package, test package, testng-{app}.xml.
- CI auto-discovers new modules via `ls apps/`.
- Config: EnvironmentConfig merges app config with framework defaults via priority cascade: sysprop > env > app config > defaults.
- No code duplication: Common UI (Header, Footer, Navigation) in test-commons. Cross-app workflows in test-commons.

5. FLAKY DETECTION:
- Detection: RetryAnalyzer tracks flaky cache. Test is flaky if it fails at least once but eventually passes. Flakiness rate tracked over last 10 runs in ELK.
- Quarantine: QuarantineManager reads quarantine.yaml from Git. Tests with >20% flakiness over 30 runs auto-quarantined to separate suite. PR must de-quarantine.
- Reporting: Slack notification daily with flaky test list. Allure shows @Flaky badge.

6. SECRETS INJECTION:
- Vault stores secrets at secret/qa/{app}/{env}/{key}. Vault agent sidecar writes to tmpfs volume. @InjectSecret annotation reads from file into char[] (zeroed after use).
- SecretMaskingAppender regex-masks secrets in logs (e.g., "Bearer [a-zA-Z0-9._-]+").
- @Secret annotated fields excluded from Allure environment blocks and CLI help.
- Screenshots scanned for secret patterns before upload.

title: Microservices Event-Driven Testing Strategy with Kafka/RabbitMQ/SQS
prompt:
Design a comprehensive testing strategy for a microservices architecture with:
- 40 services across 6 domains (Payment, Order, Inventory, Shipping, Notification, User)
- Async event-driven communication via Kafka, RabbitMQ, and SQS
- Event sourcing with CQRS
- 15 event types
- 3 message brokers
- Stateful services (PostgreSQL + MongoDB)

Requirements:
- Test end-to-end flows spanning 4-5 services and 8-10 events
- Validate eventual consistency (5s SLA)
- Validate idempotency
- Validate DLQ handling
- Chaos engineering (network partitions, broker failures, consumer crashes)
- Performance: 1,000 events/sec throughput

Provide: test architecture, timing/consistency assertions, idempotency testing, DLQ validation, chaos injection, event lineage tracking.
answer:
1. TEST ARCHITECTURE:
```
Test Framework (Java/TestNG)
|-- EventOrchestrator
|   |-- KafkaEventProducer: publish to test topics (fixed partition 0 for ordering)
|   |-- KafkaEventConsumer: subscribe with test consumer group
|   |-- RabbitMQCommandProducer: push to queues
|   |-- RabbitMQListener: listen on response queues
|   `-- SQSPoller: poll SQS for notifications
|-- StateVerifier
|   |-- PostgreSQL assertions per service schema
|   |-- MongoDB assertions
|   `-- CorrelationId tracker (lineage tracing)
|-- IdempotencyInjector
|   |-- Duplicate event publisher (same key, payload, 5x)
|   `-- Exactly-once verifier (SELECT COUNT(*) = 1)
|-- DLQValidator
|   |-- Consumer simulator that throws on specific events
|   `-- DLQ poller (Kafka __consumer_offsets, RabbitMQ DLX, SQS DLQ)
|-- ChaosEngine
|   |-- iptables network partition
|   |-- SIGKILL consumer during processing
|   |-- tc netem latency injection
|   `-- Partition leader kill
`-- AssertionEngine
    |-- Eventually: poll DB with backoff 100ms->3.2s (5s SLA)
    `-- EventOrderVerifier: sequence numbers in partition
```

2. EVENT ORDERING AND CONSISTENCY:
- Ordering: Publish all test events to partition 0 (fixed key = test-correlation-id). Assert consumption order via sequence numbers.
- Timing: Eventually wrapper polls DB with exponential backoff. Assert all 4 service DBs converge within 5s SLA. Assert correlation ID across all databases.
- Consistency: After event flow, query ALL involved DBs. Payment: PAID. Order: CONFIRMED. Inventory: reserved=1. Shipping: PENDING. All 4 must match.

3. IDEMPOTENCY:
- Publish same event 5x with same key + payload. After 5s settling, assert SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE correlation_id = X is 1 in ALL service DBs.
- Test out-of-order delivery: Consume event, delay second, NACK first -- service must handle re-delivery without double processing.

4. DLQ VALIDATION:
- Deploy test consumer with maxRetries=3 that throws RuntimeException on specific event types.
- Assert: DLQ count=1, headers preserved (correlationId, retryCount=3), original offset NOT advanced.
- For SQS: assert RedrivePolicy moves to DLQ. For RabbitMQ: assert x-death header contains reason=rejected.

5. CHAOS INJECTION:
- Network partition: iptables DROP to broker-2 for 30s. Assert rebalance completes, all partitions reassigned. After rule removal, assert rejoined.
- Consumer crash: SIGKILL consumer during processing. Assert another consumer picks up uncommitted offsets (via rebalance) and re-processes exactly once.
- Latency: tc netem 2000ms+500ms on RabbitMQ. Assert publisher confirms timeout, retry fires, event eventually arrives. Assert queue depth does not exceed threshold.
- Partition leader: Kill Kafka partition leader. Assert new leader elected within session.timeout.ms. Assert acks=all ensures no data loss.

6. EVENT LINEAGE TRACKING:
- Each test generates unique correlation UUID propagated in every event header.
- LineageTracker records: eventType, topic, partition, offset, timestamp, producer, consumer, headers.
- On test failure: lineage trace exported as DOT graph + sequence diagram, attached to Allure report. Failed events highlighted in red.

title: CI/CD Pipeline Architecture for 30-Minute 8,000-Test Execution
prompt:
Design a CI/CD pipeline for:
- 8,000 tests (UI + API + Integration)
- 6 environments (dev, qa, staging, perf, prod-canary, prod)
- 5 teams contributing daily
- Pipeline must complete in <30 min (currently 2 hours)
- Run on every PR
- Auto-quarantine after 3 consecutive failures
- 100 K8s pods parallel execution
- Dynamic test distribution (not static suite splitting)
- Flaky detection within 2 runs
- Test impact analysis for selective re-run
- Cost-aware scheduling

Provide: pipeline stages, impact analysis algorithm, dynamic distribution, flaky quarantine, infrastructure failure handling, cost-aware scheduling.
answer:
1. PIPELINE STAGES (30 min total):
```
Stage 1: BUILD & IMPACT (2 min)
  |-- git diff --name-only $BASE..$HEAD
  |-- TestImpactAnalyzer: map changed files to tests via dependency graph
  |-- Output: mandatory-tests.txt, optional-tests.txt, smoke-tests.txt
```
```
Stage 2: SMOKE GATE (3 min) -- 1 K8s pod, top 20 smoke tests. If fails: BLOCK PR.
```
```
Stage 3: DYNAMIC SPLIT (1 min) -- Greedy bin-packing: sort tests by duration descending, assign to 100 bins targeting 5% of mean deviation.
```
```
Stage 4: PARALLEL EXECUTION (20 min) -- 100 K8s pods each running 1 split. Each pod: 4GB RAM, 2 CPU, 1 browser slot. Results uploaded to S3.
  |-- If pod crashes: tests re-queued to standby pool.
```
```
Stage 5: AGGREGATION (3 min) -- Download 100 testng-results.xml, merge, generate Allure. Update FlakyDetector.
  |-- FlakyDetector: if test failed in 2/2 runs: FLAKY. 3/3: AUTO-QUARANTINE.
```
```
Stage 6: COST GATE (1 min) -- If cost > $50 AND trigger=PR: reduce optional tests by 50%, skip perf tests.
```

2. TEST IMPACT ANALYSIS:
- Dependency graph (build-cache/impact/graph.json) maps: Java class -> tests, SQL file -> tests, YAML config -> tests.
- Generated by @TestImpact annotation processor during main branch full build.
- Algorithm:
  1. CHANGES = git diff --name-only
  2. For each file: look up in graph. If found: add all associated tests. If not: add all smoke tests (conservative).
  3. Always add ALL_CONFIG_TESTS (YAML changes affect all tests).
- Precision: ~85%. False negatives mitigated by smoke gate.

3. DYNAMIC DISTRIBUTION:
- Greedy bin packing: sort tests by historical duration descending. Assign each to bin with minimum total time. Rebalance until all bins within 5% of mean.
- Algorithm runs in Stage 3, writes 100 split-{idx}.txt files to shared PVC.
- Each K8s pod reads its split via POD_INDEX env var (StatefulSet ordinal).

4. FLAKY DETECTION:
- Compare last 2 runs: failed in both = CONSISTENTLY FAILING. Failed in 1 = FLAKY. Failed in all 3 = AUTO-QUARANTINE.
- Quarantine: PR created to update quarantine.yaml. Tests excluded from main suite, run in daily quarantine pipeline (non-blocking).
- Un-quarantine: If a quarantined test passes 10 consecutive runs, auto-un-quarantine via PR.

5. INFRASTRUCTURE FAILURE HANDLING:
- Node failure: K8s reschedules pods on remaining nodes. Aborted tests appear as ABORTED in report, re-queued to standby pool (5 extra pods always idle).
- Broker crash: Pipeline retries failed HTTP calls (3 attempts, 5s backoff). If broker unreachable: FAIL_FAST with clear error message.
- Pod OOM: cgroup OOM killer terminates Chrome. Pod health check fails, pod restarts, tests on that pod re-executed on a different node.

6. COST-AWARE SCHEDULING:
- Cost = k8s_pod_seconds * $0.0005 + browser_minutes * $0.01.
- If trigger=PR AND cost > $50:
  - Reduce optional tests by 50%
  - Skip performance tests
  - Comment on PR: "Cost optimization applied. Run /full-suite to run all tests."
- If trigger=main OR nightly: run FULL suite regardless of cost.
- Historical test durations stored in S3 (test-historical-duration.json), updated after each run.

title: Enterprise Secrets Management and Environment Configuration Architecture
prompt:
Design a secrets management and environment configuration system for a QA automation framework spanning:
- 10 microservices, each with dev/staging/production environments
- 50+ secret values per environment (API keys, DB passwords, OAuth client secrets, TLS certs)
- 200+ non-secret config keys (URLs, timeouts, feature flags, browser settings)
- 32 parallel test threads
- CI/CD integration with GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Azure DevOps
- Local developer execution (no Vault access) using local .env files
- Allure reporting must NOT expose secrets
- Logs must mask secrets automatically
- Audit trail: which test accessed which secret at what time

Provide:
1. Complete architecture with all components and data flow
2. How secrets are fetched, cached, and injected into tests
3. How the framework distinguishes secret vs non-secret config
4. How secret values are protected in logs, reports, and stack traces
5. How it works offline (developer laptop) vs CI (Vault available)
6. How the audit trail is implemented without performance impact
answer:
1. ARCHITECTURE:
```
[Vault Server (prod)] <-- (TLS) --> [Vault Agent Sidecar] --writes to--> [/vault/secrets/ (tmpfs)]
                                                                               |
[Developer Laptop] --reads--> [.env.local]                                   [Java App]
                                                                               |
[CI/CD Pipeline] --injects--> [ENV Vars] ----reads----> [ConfigLoader]         |
                                                            |              [@InjectSecret]
                                                     [ConfigRegistry] ---> [Page Objects]
                                                            |                   |
                                                     [SecretMasker]      [Guice DI]
```

ConfigLoader priority chain (highest to lowest):
1. System properties (-Dsecret.apiKey=...)
2. Environment variables (SECRET_API_KEY)
3. Vault (from /vault/secrets/ file or directly via API)
4. .env.local file (dev laptop only, gitignored)
5. .env.default (checked into repo, contains placeholder values)

2. SECRET FETCHING, CACHING, AND INJECTION:
- At startup, ConfigLoader scans all @Config fields and resolves values using priority chain.
- Non-secret config: loaded eagerly into a ConcurrentHashMap (shared across threads).
- Secret config: loaded lazily via Vault client, cached in char[] (not String) for 5 minutes, zeroed after use.
- Vault agent sidecar (K8s): writes secrets to /vault/secrets/{path} as tmpfs. ConfigLoader reads from file (faster than API, no network).
- CI without Vault agent: falls back to environment variables injected by CI/CD (GitHub Actions secrets -> env vars).
- @InjectSecret annotation processed by Guice SPI: reads char[] from cache, injects into field, zeros after constructor completes.
- Thread safety: char[] is immutable reference but mutable contents. Each thread gets its own copy via ThreadLocal<char[]>.

3. SECRET VS NON-SECRET DISTINCTION:
- Annotation-based: @ConfigProperty (non-secret) vs @SecretConfigProperty (secret).
- Field naming convention: fields containing "password", "secret", "key", "token", "cert" are auto-classified as secret.
- YAML schema: config.yaml has two sections: public: { ... } and secret: { ... }.
- The ConfigRegistry maintains two maps: publicConfig and secretConfig. Only publicConfig is accessible for reporting.

4. SECRET PROTECTION:
- Logging: Log4j2 SecretMaskingAppender uses regex patterns:
  - "Bearer [a-zA-Z0-9._-]+" -> "Bearer ***"
  - "(password|secret|apiKey)":"[^"]+" -> "$1":"***"
  - Any field tagged @Secret is masked in toString() by a custom Jackson serializer.
- Allure: Environment block only includes @ConfigProperty fields (not @SecretConfigProperty). Screenshot OCR-scan before upload (skip if secret visible).
- Stack traces: ExceptionUtils (Apache Commons) filters stack frames containing secret values. @Secret field values replaced with "[REDACTED]" in error messages.
- Heap dumps: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError disabled in test runners. If enabled, secrets are in char[] and harder to find than String (but not impossible).

5. OFFLINE VS CI:
- Developer laptop: ConfigLoader reads from .env.local (gitignored). If file missing, falls back to .env.default with placeholder values. Developer can also set system properties in IDE run config.
- CI: Vault agent available in CI runner pod. ConfigLoader reads /vault/secrets/ directory. If Vault unavailable (network issue), falls back to CI/CD injected environment variables.
- All three CI systems (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Azure DevOps) inject secrets as environment variables using their respective secret stores (GitHub Actions secrets, Jenkins credentials, Azure Key Vault).

6. AUDIT TRAIL:
- AuditAspect (Guice AOP interceptor) wraps all @InjectSecret and getSecret() calls.
- Records: secret path, thread ID, test name, timestamp, caller stack trace (first 3 frames).
- Buffered writes: audit entries written to a ConcurrentLinkedQueue. Flushed asynchronously every 10 seconds to an audit.log file (not sent over network to avoid perf impact).
- In CI: audit.log is uploaded as a pipeline artifact only on test failure. On success, only summary (number of secrets accessed) is logged.
- Performance: <0.1ms per secret access (in-memory queue + async flush). No lock contention (ConcurrentLinkedQueue).

title: Flaky Test Root Causes in Selenium Grid 4
prompt: Which of the following are VALID root causes of flaky tests in a Selenium Grid 4 setup? Select ALL that apply.
options: Implicit wait and explicit wait are used together. The implicit wait timeout is applied by the remote end on every findElement, including those internal to ExpectedConditions. Each elementToBeClickable poll takes 10s + 500ms instead of 500ms, drastically reducing effective polling frequency and making the test miss short-lived DOM states.

The Selenium Grid 4 Router component uses a least-recently-used session allocation strategy. When a test requests a new session, the Router assigns it to the node with the fewest active sessions. If one node has a slower CPU or higher latency, it receives more sessions than it can handle, causing timeouts that the Router doesn't account for.

Selenium 4's W3C protocol requires the client to serialize element references as maps with a specific UUID key. If the test code uses JSON Wire Protocol (JWP) format (element ID as string), the remote end receives an unrecognized format and throws InvalidArgumentException. This happens silently in some Grid configurations where the backward-compatibility layer is disabled.

ChromeDriver session creation involves negotiating a bidirectional CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) connection. Under high concurrency, the Node's port allocation for CDP connections fails (port range exhaustion), but the session creation returns success before the CDP handshake completes. Subsequent findElement calls fail with NoSuchSessionException from the CDP layer while the original session creation appears to have succeeded.

The maxSession parameter in the Grid node config limits the number of concurrent browser slots. When maxSession is set higher than the number of available CPU cores, the JVM's thread scheduler oversubscribes, causing thread starvation. The WebDriverWait polling mechanism relies on the main thread getting CPU time — under oversubscription, poll intervals drift from 500ms to 3-5s, causing timeouts on fast-rendering pages.

Selenium Grid 4's distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) inserts spans into every HTTP request. Under load, the span exporter queue backs up, causing the Grid components to spend more time serializing trace data than processing requests. This causes session creation to exceed the 30s timeout for some nodes while others complete normally, leading to intermittent failures.
answer: A, C, D, E

title: Thread-Safety Violations in Test Framework Code
prompt: Which of the following code patterns are DEFINITE thread-safety violations when running 32 parallel TestNG tests? Select ALL that apply.
options: A static SimpleDateFormat instance shared across all tests for date formatting. SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe and its internal calendar object can produce wrong dates or throw NumberFormatException when accessed concurrently.

A static ThreadLocal<WebDriver> with initializer that creates a new ChromeDriver. Each thread gets its own driver via ThreadLocal.get(), but the driver is never removed. After 1000 tests, the ThreadLocalMap retains 32 driver references across the thread pool, preventing GC of undead sessions.

A static AtomicInteger counter used to generate unique test data IDs. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() guarantees atomicity, but the generated ID is used in a database INSERT that may conflict with another thread's INSERT due to database-level unique constraint race.

A static HashMap<String, Boolean> used as a flaky test cache. Multiple threads call put() concurrently without synchronization. HashMap's internal modCount becomes inconsistent, causing infinite loops during rehashing and ConcurrentModificationException during iteration.

A static CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> used to collect all created test entity IDs. One thread iterates the list (forEach) while another thread adds to it. CopyOnWriteArrayList guarantees safe iteration by taking a snapshot, but the iteration sees a stale snapshot missing recently added elements.

A static ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> used for metrics counting. One thread calls computeIfAbsent() while another calls merge(). ConcurrentHashMap guarantees atomic per-key operations, but the combination of computeIfAbsent + merge on different keys is safe. However, if both threads operate on the same key, the operations are serialized correctly.
answer: A, B, D

title: Selenium Grid 4 Production Issues
prompt: Which of the following are known Selenium Grid 4 production issues that require specific configuration changes? Select ALL that apply.
options: Selenium Grid 4 by default enables basic HTTP authentication for the Grid endpoints. If the test code does not include authentication in the RemoteWebDriver URL, session creation fails with HTTP 401. The fix requires either configuring the Grid without authentication or updating all test scripts to include credentials in the URL.

The Grid 4 EventBus (used for node-registrar communication) uses a default timeout of 30 seconds. On busy networks or during node startup storms, registration can exceed this timeout, leaving nodes unregistered and unavailable to the Router. The fix requires increasing the eventbus timeout via configuration or node startup-staggering.

Selenium Grid 4 nodes expose two ports: one for the node HTTP server and one for the debug port. By default, the debug port is bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces) in Docker containers, creating a security vulnerability. The fix requires passing SE_NODE_GRID_URL or binding the debug port to localhost.

The Grid 4 NewSessionQueue has a default maximum queue size of 100 requests. Under heavy load, session requests beyond 100 are immediately rejected with a 503 response. The fix requires increasing the queue size or implementing client-side retry with backoff.

Selenium Grid 4 nodes automatically detect available browsers by scanning the PATH. If multiple versions of the same browser are installed, the node may pick the wrong version. The fix requires explicitly specifying the browser binary path in the node configuration.

Selenium Grid 4 does not support session timeouts by default. If a test acquires a session but hangs (infinite loop), the session is never released, eventually exhausting all available slots. The fix requires configuring sessionTimeout in the node config to auto-release hung sessions.
answer: B, C, D, F
